title: Nationalism and Imperialism
bigQuestion: Why did the strongest nations of the late 1800s carve up most of the world, how did the people they conquered respond, and how did it all lead toward 1914?

story.title: The Mountains at Adwa
story.kicker: On the first day of March in 1896, an Italian army marched into the hills of northern Ethiopia expecting an easy victory over an African king. It met a hundred thousand soldiers instead.
paragraphs: Before dawn on March 1, 1896, three Italian columns move through the dark hills near the town of Adwa in northern Ethiopia. They number about seventeen thousand men, Italians and African soldiers recruited in the colony of Eritrea, with dozens of artillery pieces. Their commander, General Baratieri, has been told by his government in Rome that Italy expects a victory. Italy is a new nation, united only thirty-five years earlier, and its leaders want colonies like Britain and France have. The maps the Italians carry are poor. In the dark, the columns lose touch with each other.

Waiting for them is the Emperor Menelik the Second and his Empress Taytu, with an army of roughly one hundred thousand. Menelik has spent years preparing for this day. He has bought modern rifles and artillery from the very European powers now competing in Africa, including from Italy itself. He has united rival Ethiopian lords under one banner by argument, marriage and force. His soldiers know the ground. When the Italians realize their mistake, they are already spread across three separate valleys, and the Ethiopians attack each column in turn.

By noon the battle is decided. Thousands of Italian soldiers are dead or captured. Baratieri retreats toward Eritrea with the survivors. Menelik does not chase him to the sea. He has proved his point, and his army needs food. In October Italy signs a treaty recognizing Ethiopia's full independence. In Rome, crowds riot and the prime minister resigns. Across Africa and Asia, and among Black Americans reading the news in Chicago and elsewhere, Adwa becomes a name to remember. An African state has beaten a European army in open battle and kept its freedom.

The reason it matters is what surrounds it. In 1870 Europeans controlled about a tenth of Africa. By 1914 they controlled nearly all of it, with Ethiopia and Liberia the only exceptions. In the same decades Britain ruled India directly, European powers forced China to give up ports and rights, and Japan, after remaking itself in a generation, seized its own colonies. This chapter asks how a few nations came to rule so much of the world, why they believed they had the right, what conquered peoples did about it, and how the rivalries of empire tightened into the alliances that were waiting for a spark in 1914.

Adwa also shows the two threads of the chapter tied together. Italy was at Adwa because nationalism had made it a country and its leaders wanted an empire to prove it. Ethiopia won at Adwa because Menelik had built something like a modern nation, with a unified army and modern weapons, out of his own rival provinces. Nationalism drove the conquerors and armed the resisters. Keep that in mind as the chapter moves from Italy and Germany to Japan, Africa, India, China and finally the summer of 1914.
story.think: Menelik bought his rifles from the same European countries that were competing to conquer Africa. Why would they sell them to him? What does that tell you about how empire actually worked?

lessons.title: Italy Made by Diplomacy and Volunteers
lessons.mainIdea: Italy was united between 1859 and 1870 by a combination of Cavour's careful diplomacy in the north and Garibaldi's volunteer army in the south.
reading: In 1850 Italy was, as an Austrian minister once said, only a geographical expression. The peninsula was divided into about ten states. Austria ruled the rich north around Milan and Venice. The pope ruled the middle from Rome. A Spanish-descended king ruled Naples and Sicily. Only one Italian state had a constitution and an elected parliament: the small kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia in the northwest. After the failure of 1848, Italian *nationalists* who wanted one country looked to Piedmont as the state that could lead.

Piedmont's prime minister, Count Camillo di Cavour, was a practical man who distrusted romantic revolution. He built railways, modernized the army, and looked for a powerful friend. In 1858 he made a secret deal with the French emperor Napoleon the Third: France would help drive Austria out of northern Italy in exchange for territory. War came in 1859. French and Piedmontese troops won bloody battles, and Austria gave up Lombardy, the region around Milan. Small states in central Italy then voted to join Piedmont. Cavour had won half of Italy by *diplomacy*, the art of negotiating between states, and one carefully chosen war.

The south came differently. Giuseppe Garibaldi was a soldier and a revolutionary who had fought in South America and in 1848. In May 1860 he sailed from near Genoa with about a thousand volunteers in red shirts to Sicily, where a revolt had broken out against the king of Naples. Peasants joined him. Within months his growing army had taken Sicily and Naples. Garibaldi could have set up a republic; instead he met King Victor Emmanuel of Piedmont and handed over his conquests. In March 1861 the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed. Venice was added after a war in 1866, and Rome in 1870 when French troops guarding the pope left to fight Prussia.

Unity on the map was not unity in fact. Most Italians spoke regional dialects and could not read; the standard Italian of the new state was a foreign language to many. The south was poor and resented being ruled from the north; for years the army fought what it called brigands there. The pope refused to recognize the kingdom and told Catholics not to take part in its politics. A leader of the movement is often quoted as saying that having made Italy, they now had to make Italians. That task, of turning people who shared a peninsula into a nation, took schools, railways, the draft and decades.

words.d: a person who wants their people to have a country of their own and puts that nation first
negotiation between governments to reach agreements or alliances
joining separate states into one country

look.title: The General and the Minister
look.text: Garibaldi has just conquered Sicily and Naples with a volunteer army. He is a hero to millions and a republican at heart. Cavour, the minister of a monarchy, fears that Garibaldi will march on Rome, bring France into a war, and lose everything. In the end Garibaldi hands his conquests to the king and goes home to his farm on a small island.
look.prompt: Why might Garibaldi have given up power he had won? What did each man contribute that the other could not?

check.q: Why did Italian nationalists look to Piedmont to lead unification after 1848?
choices: It was the largest state in Italy
It was ruled by the pope
It was the only Italian state with a constitution and parliament and it had a modern army
It was controlled by Austria
check.why: Piedmont-Sardinia alone had kept a constitution after 1848, and Cavour built the railways and army to make it the natural leader.

check.q: How did Cavour gain northern Italy?
choices: By a secret deal with France and a war against Austria in 1859
By leading a thousand volunteers to Milan
By buying it from Austria
By waiting for Austria to collapse
check.why: Cavour's alliance with Napoleon the Third brought French armies into a war that forced Austria to give up Lombardy.

check.q: Why does the saying 'now we must make Italians' matter?
choices: Because Italy still lacked a capital
Because Austria still ruled Rome
Because Garibaldi refused to join the kingdom
Because most Italians spoke dialects, could not read, and did not yet feel like one people
check.why: Political unification came first; building a shared language, schools and loyalty took decades more.

lessons.title: Bismarck and the German Empire
lessons.mainIdea: Otto von Bismarck united Germany under Prussia through three short wars, creating the most powerful state in Europe and a new balance of power.
reading: In 1860 the German-speaking lands were still a loose league of about thirty-nine states. Two rivals dominated them. Austria was a sprawling empire of many peoples. Prussia was a disciplined kingdom in the north with the best-drilled army in Europe. Liberals in 1848 had tried to unite Germany by a parliament and failed. In 1862 the Prussian king appointed Otto von Bismarck as his chief minister. Bismarck was a conservative landowner who despised parliaments. He believed the great questions of the day would be decided not by speeches and majority votes but by iron and blood.

He meant it. Bismarck ignored the Prussian parliament's refusal to fund the army and expanded it anyway. Then he used it three times. In 1864 Prussia and Austria together took two provinces from Denmark. In 1866 Bismarck picked a quarrel with Austria over those provinces, and Prussia's army, using railways and new breech-loading rifles, crushed the Austrians in seven weeks. Prussia annexed several northern states and formed a North German Confederation without Austria. Bismarck made the peace deliberately mild, so Austria would not seek revenge.

France was the last obstacle. Bismarck knew the southern German states, Catholic and suspicious of Prussia, would only join if they faced a common enemy. In 1870 he edited a diplomatic telegram to make it sound as if the French ambassador and the Prussian king had insulted each other. France, under Napoleon the Third, declared war. The southern states joined Prussia, and the German armies trapped the French at Sedan in September and captured the emperor. On January 18, 1871, in the Hall of Mirrors at the French palace of Versailles, the German princes proclaimed the Prussian king *Kaiser*, emperor, of a united Germany.

The new German Empire took the French provinces of Alsace and Lorraine, a wound France never forgot. It had the largest population in Europe west of Russia and the fastest-growing industry. Its constitution gave the Kaiser and his chancellor most of the power. Bismarck now called Germany a satisfied state. He spent twenty years building alliances to keep France isolated and the peace intact. The map of Europe had been redrawn by *realpolitik*, politics based on power and results rather than ideals. Nationalism, which liberals had hoped would free peoples, had been harnessed by a conservative to build a military empire.

words.d: the German word for emperor, used for the ruler of the German Empire from 1871 to 1918
politics based on practical power and results rather than ideals or morals
to take territory and make it part of your own country

look.title: Iron and Blood
look.text: Speaking to a parliamentary committee in 1862, Bismarck argued that Prussia's place in Germany would not be won by liberal ideals. The great questions of the time, he said, would be settled not by speeches and majority decisions, which he called the mistake of 1848, but by iron and blood.
look.cite: Otto von Bismarck, speech to the Prussian budget committee, September 1862 (translated and paraphrased)
look.prompt: What is Bismarck saying about the liberals of 1848? Judging by what he did over the next nine years, was he right about how Germany would be united?

check.q: What did Bismarck mean by settling questions with iron and blood?
choices: That Germany should build more steel mills
That parliaments should vote on war
That Prussia should ally with Austria
That unification would come through military force, not speeches and votes
check.why: Bismarck rejected the liberal approach of 1848 and used the Prussian army in three wars to unite Germany.

check.q: Why did Bismarck want a war with France in 1870?
choices: To capture Paris permanently
Because a common enemy would bring the southern German states into union with Prussia
Because France had invaded Prussia
To free Alsace from Austrian rule
check.why: The Catholic southern states distrusted Prussia but joined it against France, and unification followed victory.

check.q: How did the German Empire's constitution distribute power?
choices: Most power went to the Kaiser and chancellor rather than the elected parliament
All power went to an elected assembly
Each state kept full independence
The pope chose the chancellor
check.why: Germany had an elected Reichstag, but the emperor and his chancellor controlled the army and foreign policy.

lessons.title: Japan Remakes Itself
lessons.mainIdea: After being forced open by American warships, Japan's Meiji leaders overturned their old order and built a modern state strong enough to defeat a European empire by 1905.
reading: In July 1853 four American warships under Commodore Matthew Perry steamed into Edo Bay, near the city now called Tokyo. Two were steam-powered and belched black smoke. Japan had shut itself off from most foreign contact for over two centuries under the *shogun*, the military ruler who governed in the emperor's name. Perry carried a letter demanding that Japan open its ports. He returned the next year with more ships, and the shogun's government, knowing it could not fight, signed a treaty. Soon Britain, Russia and others forced similar unequal treaties that let foreigners trade and be tried by their own courts.

Many Japanese saw the treaties as humiliation and blamed the shogun. In 1868 a group of young samurai from outlying domains overthrew the shogunate and declared that they were restoring power to the fifteen-year-old emperor, who took the reign name Meiji, meaning enlightened rule. The Meiji Restoration was a revolution from above. The new leaders abolished the old domains and the privileges of the samurai class, including their right to wear swords. They created a draft army of commoners, a national school system, and a modern tax on land. Their slogan was rich country, strong army.

They studied the West with a purpose. The Iwakura mission of 1871 to 1873 sent about fifty leaders around the United States and Europe to see how modern states worked. Japan hired foreign experts, then replaced them with Japanese once the skills were learned. It adopted a written constitution in 1889 modeled partly on Germany's, with an elected lower house but power concentrated in the emperor's ministers. Railways, telegraphs, shipyards and textile mills followed. Japanese leaders adopted Western clothes, calendars and law codes while insisting on Japanese loyalty to the emperor.

The test came in war. In 1894 and 1895 Japan defeated China and took Taiwan. In 1904 and 1905 it fought Russia over control of Korea and Manchuria, destroyed the Russian fleet in a single battle, and won. It was the first time in modern history that an Asian state had defeated a European great power, and nationalists from India to Egypt took notice. Japan renegotiated the unequal treaties and in 1910 annexed Korea outright. The country that had been forced open in 1853 was, half a century later, an *imperial* power itself, ruling other peoples as Europeans did.

words.d: the military ruler who governed Japan in the emperor's name until 1868
returning power to a ruler; in Japan, the 1868 return of power to the emperor
relating to an empire, a state that rules other territories and peoples

look.title: Black Ships in the Bay
look.text: A fisherman in 1853 looks up from his boat and sees four enormous ships moving against the wind, trailing black smoke, with guns along their sides larger than any in Japan. Word spreads that the foreigners demand the ports be opened. Some samurai want to fight them at once. Others argue that fighting is hopeless and that Japan must learn what makes those ships possible.
look.prompt: Which response did Japan's leaders eventually choose, and what would fighting have cost? What did learning cost instead?

check.q: Why did Japan sign the treaty Perry demanded in 1854?
choices: The emperor admired the United States
Japan wanted to sell silk to America
The shogun's government knew it could not defeat modern warships
Japan had always welcomed foreign trade
check.why: Facing steam warships with heavy guns, the shogunate concluded that resistance was hopeless and signed.

check.q: Which change was part of the Meiji reforms?
choices: Restoring the shogun's power
Creating a draft army of commoners and ending samurai privileges
Closing all ports to foreigners
Abolishing the emperor
check.why: The Meiji leaders dismantled the samurai class and built a national army, schools and tax system on Western models.

check.q: Why did Japan's 1905 victory over Russia matter beyond Japan?
choices: It ended all European empires
It gave Japan control of Siberia
It made Russia an ally of Japan
It showed nationalists across Asia that a non-European state could defeat a European great power
check.why: The war was the first modern victory of an Asian nation over a European empire, and it inspired movements from India to Egypt.

lessons.title: Berlin Draws the Lines
lessons.mainIdea: Between 1870 and 1914 European powers divided nearly all of Africa among themselves, setting the rules at a conference in Berlin to which no African was invited.
reading: In 1870 European rule in Africa was mostly a fringe of coastal forts and trading posts, plus French Algeria in the north and British and Dutch settlers in the south. Inside the continent, hundreds of African states, kingdoms and peoples governed themselves. Then, in less than thirty years, Europeans claimed almost everything. Historians call it the *scramble* for Africa, because that is how it looked: a rush, each power grabbing land before a rival could. By 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent.

Several things made the scramble possible. Quinine, a medicine from a South American tree bark, let Europeans survive malaria in the interior. Steamboats went up rivers that sailing ships could not. The telegraph carried orders from Europe in hours. Above all, new rifles and the Maxim machine gun, which could fire hundreds of rounds a minute, gave small European forces an overwhelming advantage over larger African armies armed with older guns or spears. At the battle of Omdurman in Sudan in 1898, British forces with machine guns killed about ten thousand Sudanese soldiers while losing fewer than fifty of their own.

The rush created quarrels among the Europeans, and in 1884 Bismarck invited the powers to Berlin to set rules. The Berlin Conference met from November 1884 to February 1885. Fourteen states attended; not one African ruler or representative was invited. The delegates agreed that a power claiming a coast had to actually occupy it to keep it, and they recognized King Leopold the Second of Belgium's personal claim to the vast Congo basin. Then they went home and sent soldiers to sign treaties, often in languages the African signers could not read, that turned trade agreements into surrenders of sovereignty.

The borders drawn in these years were lines on maps made by men who had mostly never been to Africa. Rivers, straight lines and lines of latitude split peoples in two and forced rivals into one *colony*. Those borders largely survive today as the borders of African nations, and many of the continent's later conflicts run along them. The scramble was quick, and it was not in any sense agreed to by the people whose land it divided. That fact, more than any other, shaped what came after.

words.d: a frantic rush to grab something before others do; here, the European race to claim Africa
a territory ruled by a distant country, usually for that country's benefit
a medicine from tree bark that prevents and treats malaria

look.title: Africa Under European Control
look.unit: rough percent of Africa's land, rounded
look.prompt: In which period did control jump the most? What happened in 1884 and 1885 that helps explain the jump?

check.q: Which technology most directly gave small European forces an advantage in African battles?
choices: The telegraph
Steam-powered mills
The machine gun and modern rifles
Railways
check.why: Rapid-firing weapons let a few hundred European troops defeat armies many times their size, as at Omdurman in 1898.

check.q: Who was not at the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885?
choices: Germany
Any African ruler or representative
Britain
Belgium's king's representatives
check.why: Fourteen European and American states set the rules for dividing Africa without a single African present.

check.q: Why do the borders drawn in the scramble still matter?
choices: They were redrawn completely after 1914
They followed the borders of African kingdoms exactly
They were never used
They became the borders of today's African nations, splitting some peoples and forcing rivals together
check.why: Lines drawn in Europe with little knowledge of Africa were kept after independence and shape many later conflicts.

lessons.title: Why Empire: Motives and Excuses
lessons.mainIdea: Europeans took empires for profit, power and prestige, and justified them with claims about race, religion and civilization that many people at the time also challenged.
reading: Ask why a country would spend money and lives to rule people thousands of miles away, and you get several answers, all partly true. The first is *economic*. Factories needed raw materials such as cotton, rubber, palm oil and copper, and they needed markets to sell to. Investors wanted places to put their capital. Yet the numbers are mixed: most European trade was with other industrial countries, not colonies, and many colonies cost more to run than they returned. Empire made some companies and individuals very rich while taxpayers paid the bills.

The second answer is power and pride. After 1871 Germany, Italy and a Britain worried about German growth all measured themselves by territory on the map. A coaling station for warships, a port on a strategic strait, a colony to deny a rival: strategy drove much of the scramble. Newspapers sold papers with stories of explorers and battles, and voters cheered flags on maps. A politician who lost a colonial contest could lose an election. Nationalism, which had built Italy and Germany, now demanded that every real nation have an empire.

The third answer is the set of ideas Europeans used to explain themselves. Missionaries wanted to spread Christianity and often built schools and hospitals. Others spoke of a duty to bring civilization, meaning European law, medicine and trade, to people they considered backward. The English writer Rudyard Kipling called this the white man's burden in an 1899 poem urging the United States to rule the Philippines. Some thinkers twisted Darwin's science into a claim that races competed like species and that Europeans had proved themselves fittest. Scientists today reject this entirely, and many people rejected it then.

Critics spoke up in Europe and America. The economist J. A. Hobson argued in 1902 that empire benefited a few investors at everyone else's expense. Mark Twain and other members of the Anti-Imperialist League attacked the American war in the Philippines. Missionaries and a British consul named Roger Casement exposed the horrors of Leopold's Congo. And colonized people themselves answered most sharply: an Indian lawyer, an Egyptian journalist or an Ethiopian emperor could point out that if civilization meant law and consent, empire by conquest was its opposite. The justifications did not convince everyone even in their own day.

words.d: having to do with money, trade, resources and jobs
a person sent to spread a religion, often also running schools or hospitals
respect and standing in the eyes of others, often a motive for empire

look.title: The Burden and Its Critics
look.text: Kipling's 1899 poem urged Americans to take up what he called the white man's burden: to send their best young men into exile to serve the needs of newly conquered peoples, whom he described as half devil and half child, and to expect only blame and hatred in return. Anti-imperialists in the United States answered with parodies and with the argument that a republic founded on consent could not rule others by force.
look.cite: Rudyard Kipling, The White Man's Burden, 1899, and responses by the American Anti-Imperialist League (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Kipling presents empire as a sacrifice by the conqueror. What does his poem assume about the conquered? How would a Filipino or Indian reader have answered?

check.q: What does the lesson say about the claim that colonies were profitable?
choices: Every colony made its ruling country rich
Only Germany profited from empire
Colonies were never about money
Some companies and individuals profited, but many colonies cost taxpayers more than they returned
check.why: Most European trade was with other industrial nations, and empire enriched a few while the public paid for soldiers and administration.

check.q: How did nationalism feed imperialism after 1871?
choices: Nations measured their greatness by colonies on the map and voters cheered expansion
Nationalists opposed all empires
Nationalism ended after unification
Nationalists wanted only economic ties with Africa
check.why: New and old powers alike treated colonies as proof of national strength, and losing a colonial contest could cost an election.

check.q: Which of these was a critic of empire in its own time?
choices: Rudyard Kipling
King Leopold the Second
The Anti-Imperialist League, including Mark Twain
General Baratieri
check.why: The Anti-Imperialist League attacked the American conquest of the Philippines, showing the justifications were disputed even then.

lessons.title: Rubber, Resistance and Adwa
lessons.mainIdea: Colonial rule in Africa ranged from brutal forced labor in the Congo to indirect rule elsewhere, and Africans resisted by war, by revolt and by organizing, with Ethiopia keeping its independence.
reading: The Congo Free State showed empire at its worst. King Leopold the Second of Belgium held it as his personal property from 1885 to 1908, and he wanted profit from wild rubber. His agents set quotas for villages. Men were sent into the forest to tap rubber vines; if a village fell short, soldiers took women and children hostage, burned homes, or cut off hands as proof of punishment. Missionaries photographed the victims. The British consul Roger Casement's 1904 report and a campaign led by the journalist E. D. Morel forced Belgium's parliament to take the colony from the king in 1908. The population of the region fell by millions in those years, from killing, famine and disease.

Most colonies were not the Congo, but all rested on force. Britain often used *indirect rule*, governing through existing chiefs and kings who kept their titles but took orders. France tried to make Africans in some colonies into French citizens, a promise kept for very few. Everywhere, colonial governments demanded taxes paid in cash, which pushed Africans to work for wages in mines and on plantations, and they took the best land for European settlers in places like Kenya and Algeria. Railways ran from mines to ports, not between African cities. The economy was built to serve the ruling country.

Africans fought back from the beginning. Samori Touré built an empire in West Africa and fought the French for more than fifteen years before his capture in 1898. The Zulu army destroyed a British force at Isandlwana in 1879 before being crushed months later. In German East Africa, the Maji Maji rising of 1905 to 1907 united many peoples against forced cotton growing; German troops answered with a famine campaign that killed tens of thousands. In Southwest Africa the German army drove the Herero people into the desert to die, an act now recognized as *genocide*. Armed resistance mostly lost against machine guns, but it was everywhere.

Ethiopia was the exception, and its victory at Adwa in 1896 explains why. Menelik the Second had done what Japan did: he used the rivalry of the European powers to buy modern weapons, unified rival lords, and met the invader with an army that was larger, better led and better armed than the Italians expected. Resistance also took new forms as colonial rule settled in. Mission-educated Africans founded newspapers, formed associations and petitioned for rights in the language of the rulers. In 1912 a group in South Africa founded the organization that became the African National Congress. The struggle that would end European rule in the 1950s and 1960s had begun.

words.d: governing a colony through local chiefs or kings who keep their titles but follow the colonial power's orders
the deliberate destruction of a whole people
a fixed amount that must be produced or delivered

look.title: The Armies at Adwa, 1896
look.prompt: Numbers alone did not decide most colonial battles; machine guns beat larger armies at Omdurman. What else did Menelik have that most African rulers did not?

check.q: What forced Belgium's parliament to take the Congo from King Leopold in 1908?
choices: A war with Germany
Reports and photographs of atrocities publicized by Casement, Morel and missionaries
A drop in the price of rubber
A request from Leopold himself
check.why: Evidence of hostage-taking, mutilation and mass death, spread by a public campaign, shamed Belgium into ending Leopold's personal rule.

check.q: How did colonial governments push Africans into wage labor?
choices: By offering high wages
By building railways between African cities
By requiring taxes to be paid in cash, which meant working in mines or plantations to get it
By ending all farming
check.why: Cash taxes and the taking of land forced people who had lived by farming to work for European employers.

check.q: What did Ethiopia and Japan have in common in this era?
choices: Both were colonies of Britain
Both were defeated by Italy
Both refused to buy foreign weapons
Both used modern weapons and unified states to defeat a European power and stay independent
check.why: Menelik and the Meiji leaders each built modern armies with weapons bought from Europe and beat a European power in battle.

lessons.title: India Under the Company and the Crown
lessons.mainIdea: A trading company came to rule India, a massive rebellion in 1857 nearly ended that rule, and afterward the British Crown governed India directly for ninety years.
reading: For a century before 1857, much of India was ruled not by the British government but by a business: the East India Company. The company had come to trade in cloth, spices and tea. It built forts and hired Indian soldiers called *sepoys*. Step by step it took over provinces as the Mughal Empire weakened. By the 1850s the company governed most of the subcontinent. Its army had about two hundred thousand sepoys commanded by a few thousand British officers. It collected taxes, ran courts and annexed states whose rulers died without an heir it recognized.

In 1857 the sepoys rose. The spark was a new rifle cartridge said to be greased with cow and pig fat, which soldiers had to bite open; cow fat was forbidden to Hindus and pig fat to Muslims. The deeper causes were years of annexations, high taxes, disrespect for Indian religion and custom, and fear that the British meant to convert everyone to Christianity. Sepoys at Meerut killed their officers in May 1857 and marched to Delhi, where they proclaimed the elderly Mughal emperor their leader. Peasants, landlords and the rulers of some states joined. For over a year northern India was at war.

The fighting was savage on both sides. Rebels killed British men, women and children at Kanpur. When British and loyal Indian troops retook cities, they hanged and shot thousands, sometimes whole villages, and blew captured rebels from the mouths of cannons. The British called it the Mutiny; many Indians later called it the First War of Independence. Neither name captures everything: it was a soldiers' revolt, a peasant rising and a last stand of old rulers at once, and it never spread to the south or won over the Sikh and Gurkha troops the British relied on. By 1858 it was over.

The consequences lasted. Parliament abolished the East India Company and the British Crown took over; in 1877 Queen Victoria was named Empress of India. The period is called the *Raj*, from a Hindi word for rule. The British rebuilt the army with more British troops and units drawn from groups they considered loyal. They stopped pushing religious change but also stopped trusting Indians with power. Railways, telegraphs, canals and English-language schools followed, built for British needs and used by Indians for their own. In 1885 educated Indians founded the Indian National Congress to ask, politely at first, for a share in governing their own country.

words.d: an Indian soldier serving in the army of the East India Company or the British
British rule over India from 1858 to 1947, from a Hindi word for rule
the taking of territory into another state's control

look.title: One Event, Two Names
look.text: British writers in the 1800s called what happened in 1857 the Indian Mutiny: soldiers breaking their oath. Indian nationalists in the 1900s called it the First War of Independence: a people rising against foreign rule. Historians today note that both sepoys and civilians took part, that many Indians fought on the British side, and that the rebels had no single goal beyond ending company rule.
look.prompt: What does each name assume about who was in the right? What name would you give the event, and why?

check.q: Who governed most of India before 1857?
choices: The East India Company, a business
The British Parliament directly
The Mughal emperor
A council of Indian princes
check.why: The trading company had built an army and taken over provinces until it ruled most of the subcontinent.

check.q: Why did the greased cartridges set off the rebellion?
choices: They made the rifles misfire
The sepoys wanted British rifles instead
They were more expensive than old cartridges
Biting fat from cows or pigs violated Hindu and Muslim religious rules, on top of years of grievances
check.why: The cartridges offended both religions and confirmed fears that the British disrespected Indian faith and custom.

check.q: What changed after 1858?
choices: India became fully independent
The company expanded its rule
The Mughal emperor regained power
The British Crown took over from the company and Queen Victoria later became Empress of India
check.why: Parliament ended company rule and began the Raj, direct rule by the Crown that lasted until 1947.

lessons.title: China's Century of Humiliation
lessons.mainIdea: From the Opium War of 1839 to the Boxer uprising of 1900, foreign powers forced China to give up ports, rights and land, while the Qing dynasty weakened from within.
reading: In 1800 China under the Qing dynasty was the largest and one of the richest states on earth. It sold tea, silk and porcelain to Europe and wanted little in return except silver. British merchants found something the Chinese would buy: *opium*, an addictive drug grown in British India. By the 1830s millions of Chinese were addicted, silver was flowing out, and the emperor ordered the trade stopped. In 1839 an official named Lin Zexu seized and destroyed about twenty thousand chests of British opium at Canton. Britain sent warships.

The Opium War of 1839 to 1842 showed the gap in military technology. British steam gunboats and disciplined troops defeated Chinese forces at will. The Treaty of Nanjing in 1842 forced China to open five ports to foreign trade, pay a large sum, and hand the island of Hong Kong to Britain. It was the first of what Chinese call the *unequal treaties*. Later treaties gave foreigners the right to be tried by their own courts, opened more ports, legalized opium, and allowed missionaries anywhere. France, Russia, Germany, the United States and Japan all demanded and received similar rights.

China's troubles were also internal. The Taiping Rebellion of 1850 to 1864 was led by a man who believed he was the younger brother of Jesus. It built a rival state in southern China. Crushing it took years of war that killed, by standard estimates, twenty million people or more. The Qing court was divided. Reformers wanted Western arms and factories; conservatives saw such things as corruption. In 1895 Japan, which had reformed, defeated China in a short war and took Taiwan. European powers then carved out spheres of influence, regions where each claimed special rights. Chinese cartoons showed the country as a melon being sliced.

In 1899 and 1900 a secret society whose members practiced martial arts, called Boxers by foreigners, rose in northern China against missionaries, Chinese Christians and everything foreign. The empress dowager Cixi backed them, and Boxers besieged the foreign legations in Beijing for fifty-five days. An army from eight nations, including the United States and Japan, marched in, relieved the siege, looted the capital and imposed a huge payment. The dynasty was finished in all but name. In 1911 a revolution ended it, and in 1912 China became a republic, weak and divided but no longer an empire. Chinese today still call the years from 1839 to 1949 the century of humiliation.

words.d: an addictive drug made from poppies, sold by British merchants to China in the 1800s
an agreement forced on a weaker country that gives special rights to the stronger one
a region where an outside power claims special trading and political rights

look.title: A Letter to the Queen
look.text: In 1839 Lin Zexu drafted a letter to Queen Victoria. He asked how Britain, which forbade opium at home, could allow its merchants to sell the drug to China. He argued that the tea, silk and rhubarb China sent abroad were goods that did good, while opium did only harm, and he appealed to her conscience to stop the trade.
look.cite: Lin Zexu, letter to Queen Victoria, 1839 (translated and paraphrased)
look.prompt: Lin appeals to fairness and conscience. Britain answered with warships. What does that tell you about how disputes between unequal powers were settled in this era?

check.q: Why did British merchants sell opium to China?
choices: The Chinese emperor requested it
It was the one product Chinese buyers wanted, and it reversed the flow of silver
It was used to make tea
Britain wanted to stop Indian farmers from growing it
check.why: China sold much and bought little, so opium from British India became the way to pay for tea and pull silver out of China.

check.q: Which was a term of the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842?
choices: China handed Hong Kong to Britain and opened five ports
Britain agreed to stop the opium trade
China gained control of India
Japan received Taiwan
check.why: The first unequal treaty took Hong Kong, opened ports and imposed a payment; later treaties added more rights for foreigners.

check.q: What was the result of the Boxer uprising?
choices: China drove all foreigners out
The Qing dynasty grew stronger
An eight-nation army occupied Beijing and imposed a huge payment, leaving the dynasty near collapse
Japan was expelled from China
check.why: The foreign relief army crushed the Boxers, looted the capital and demanded payment, and the dynasty fell in 1911.

lessons.title: Living Under Empire
lessons.mainIdea: Empire changed daily life for the ruled through law, school, work and disease, and colonized people used the rulers' own tools and ideas to challenge them.
reading: What did empire feel like to the people ruled? Start with a farmer in India in the 1870s. He now paid taxes in cash on a fixed schedule, whatever the harvest. To get cash he grew cotton or indigo for export instead of food. When the rains failed, as they did in 1876 and again in the 1890s, grain was still shipped out by rail to pay debts, and millions starved in *famines* that officials recorded in detail but did little to stop. British economists at the time argued that relief would spoil the poor. Indian writers such as Dadabhai Naoroji argued that Britain was draining India's wealth. Historians still debate the numbers, but the deaths are not in doubt.

Now start with a boy in a mission school in West Africa or Vietnam. He learns to read, in French or English, and he learns that his own history is savage and his rulers' history is glorious. He may become a clerk, a teacher or a lawyer, better paid than his parents and barred from the top jobs, which are reserved for Europeans. He may be tried by different courts than a European, barred from certain clubs, made to step off the sidewalk. The *color line*, the rule that race decided rights, ran through every colony. It also ran through the United States of the same years, and Black American writers noticed the connection.

Empire brought railways, hospitals, vaccines and printed books, and defenders of empire point to them. Critics answer that these were built for the rulers' needs and paid for by the ruled. The same decades saw famines and forced labor, and Japan built railways without being colonized. Both sides are describing real things. What is harder to argue with is *consent*. No colony voted to be ruled. In every colony the government answered to a capital thousands of miles away rather than to the people it taxed.

The clerk and the lawyer became the empire's problem. Educated in the rulers' language, they read the rulers' own books about liberty and asked why the words did not apply to them. Gandhi, trained as a lawyer in London, began organizing Indians against racial laws in South Africa in the 1890s. Journalists in Cairo, Lagos and Hanoi printed newspapers. Students went abroad and met each other. When the next chapter of world history opened in 1914, the empires looked permanent on the map. The people who would take them apart were already at school.

words.d: a severe shortage of food that causes widespread hunger and death
the rule, written or unwritten, that a person's race decides their rights and place
agreement; in politics, the idea that rule is legitimate only if the ruled accept it

look.title: Two Ledgers
look.text: Imagine two account books for India in 1900. One lists what Britain built: about twenty-five thousand miles of railway, canals, telegraph lines, universities, a court system. The other lists what India paid: taxes that funded the British army in India and abroad, famines in which millions died while grain was exported, and a rule that no Indian could hold the highest posts.
look.prompt: Can the two ledgers be added up to a single answer about whether empire was good or bad for India? What is missing from both lists?

check.q: Why did Indian farmers grow cotton or indigo instead of food under British rule?
choices: Food crops would not grow in India
Cotton was easier to grow than rice
The British paid them to stop farming
They needed cash to pay fixed taxes, and export crops brought cash
check.why: Cash taxes on a fixed schedule pushed farmers toward crops they could sell, leaving them vulnerable when rains failed.

check.q: What does the lesson mean by the color line?
choices: The border between colonies
A railway between two ports
The rule that a person's race decided their rights and place in a colony
A line of latitude on the map
check.why: In every colony, and in the United States of the same era, race determined courts, jobs and where a person could go.

check.q: Why were educated colonial subjects a problem for the empires?
choices: They refused to learn European languages
They all moved to Europe
They could not find any jobs
They read the rulers' own ideas about liberty and demanded that those ideas apply to them
check.why: Lawyers, clerks and journalists trained in the rulers' schools used that training to organize and argue against colonial rule.

lessons.title: Alliances and Arms
lessons.mainIdea: Between 1879 and 1907 Europe divided into two armed alliance blocs, so that a quarrel between any two powers threatened to pull in all of them.
reading: After 1871 Bismarck's goal was to keep France, which wanted Alsace and Lorraine back, without friends. He allied Germany with Austria-Hungary in 1879, added Italy in 1882 to form the Triple Alliance, and kept a separate understanding with Russia. It was a juggling act, and it depended on him. In 1890 a new young Kaiser, Wilhelm the Second, dismissed Bismarck and let the Russian agreement lapse. France saw its chance. By 1894 France and Russia were allies, and Germany faced potential enemies on two sides, exactly what Bismarck had worked to prevent.

Britain had stayed apart, protected by the sea and the largest navy in the world. Then Germany began building a battle fleet. Wilhelm wanted a navy to match Germany's new industrial power and colonial ambitions; Britain saw it as a threat to its survival, since Britain imported most of its food by sea. The naval *arms race* took off. In 1906 Britain launched HMS Dreadnought, a battleship so fast and heavily armed that every older warship became outdated overnight, and both countries raced to build more. Britain settled its old colonial quarrels with France in 1904 and with Russia in 1907. Europe now had two blocs: the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente.

Armies grew too. Every continental power except Britain drafted young men for two or three years of service, then kept them as reserves. Russia's peacetime army was well over a million men. Germany and France each had hundreds of thousands and could call up millions. Generals drew detailed plans that depended on railway timetables. Germany's plan aimed to knock out France in six weeks before Russia could fully mobilize. *Mobilization*, calling up reserves and moving them by rail to the frontier, was so complex that once begun it was hard to stop. Any country that started later might lose before fighting began.

Add the pressures of the earlier lessons. Nationalism made governments afraid to look weak. Empire gave the powers places to collide, in Morocco in 1905 and 1911, where Germany challenged France and backed down, leaving bitterness. Newspapers in every capital printed stories of enemy plots. None of this made war certain. The powers had backed away from several crises. But the system had become one in which a small war could not stay small, because each ally had promised to fight for the other, and each general staff had a plan that could not wait.

words.d: an agreement between countries to help each other, especially in war
a competition between countries to build more and better weapons
calling up soldiers and moving them to the front to prepare for war

look.title: Two Blocs, One Map
look.text: Picture Europe in 1907. Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy are bound together in the center. France, Russia and Britain surround them on the west, east and sea. Each side has drilled its reserves and drawn up railway schedules to move them. Each side believes the other is planning to strike first.
look.prompt: If Austria-Hungary and Russia quarrel over a small country in the Balkans, which countries are pulled in, and in what order? What would a leader need in order to stop it?

check.q: What was Bismarck trying to prevent with his alliances after 1871?
choices: France finding allies and Germany facing enemies on two sides
Britain building a navy
Austria uniting with Italy
Russia industrializing
check.why: Bismarck kept France isolated and Russia friendly; after his dismissal, France and Russia allied and his fear came true.

check.q: Why did Britain see Germany's new navy as a threat?
choices: Germany had promised its fleet to France
Britain imported most of its food by sea and depended on naval control to survive
British ships were made of wood
Germany had no coastline
check.why: An island that fed itself by ship could not accept a rival fleet, so Britain launched Dreadnought and joined the Entente.

check.q: Why was mobilization hard to stop once started?
choices: Soldiers refused to go home
Trains could not be reversed
Plans depended on precise railway timetables, and a country that mobilized later risked losing before fighting began
Newspapers demanded war
check.why: Mobilization plans were so complex and time-sensitive that leaders feared any delay would hand the enemy victory.

lessons.title: A Spark Waiting
lessons.mainIdea: By 1914 the world was more connected, more armed and more divided than ever, and a murder in the Balkans set off the alliances that turned a local crisis into a world war.
reading: In 1914 a person could send a telegram from London to Bombay in minutes, buy Argentine beef in Manchester, and read in a Chicago newspaper about a riot in Cairo. Trade, investment and travel linked the world as never before. Some writers argued that war between the great powers had become impossible because it would ruin everyone's economy. Nearly all of Africa and much of Asia was ruled from Europe, and European capital, rails and warships reached everywhere. The world of 1914 was, in a sense, one system, and Europe sat at its center.

The weakest point of that system was the *Balkans*, the mountainous region of southeastern Europe. The Ottoman Empire, which had ruled it for centuries, was losing territory year by year. Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece and Romania had won independence and wanted more. Austria-Hungary, a patchwork empire of a dozen peoples, feared that Serbian nationalism would pull its own Serbs and Croats away. Russia saw itself as the protector of Serbia and other Slavic peoples. Two Balkan wars in 1912 and 1913 redrew borders and left everyone armed and angry.

On June 28, 1914, the heir to the Austrian throne, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, visited Sarajevo in Bosnia, a province Austria-Hungary had annexed in 1908 over Serbian objections. A nineteen-year-old Bosnian Serb nationalist named Gavrilo Princip, part of a small group armed with help from inside Serbia, shot him and his wife dead in their open car. Austria-Hungary, with Germany's backing, sent Serbia an *ultimatum*, a final demand with a deadline, designed to be refused. Serbia accepted most of it. Austria declared war anyway on July 28. Russia mobilized to protect Serbia. Germany declared war on Russia on August 1 and on France on August 3, invading through neutral Belgium. Britain declared war on Germany on August 4.

In five weeks a murder had become a war among all the great powers, and because those powers ruled the world, it was a world war. Soldiers from India, Senegal, Algeria, Australia, Canada and later the United States would fight in it. Historians still argue over blame: German ambition, Austrian recklessness, Russian mobilization, Serbian plotting, or a system that made everyone's fears reasonable. This chapter began with nations being made and empires being seized. It ends with those nations and empires locked into a machine that no one, in the summer of 1914, proved able to stop.

words.d: the mountainous region of southeastern Europe, including Serbia, Bosnia, Bulgaria and Greece
a final demand with a deadline, backed by a threat of force
not taking sides in a war

look.title: From Murder to World War, 1914
rows: July 28: Austria declares war on Serbia
August 1: Germany declares war on Russia
August 3: Germany declares war on France
August 4: Britain declares war on Germany
look.prompt: Notice the long pause and then the rush. What happened during the month of July, and why did the last week move so fast?

check.q: Why did Austria-Hungary fear Serbian nationalism?
choices: Serbia had a larger army than Austria
Serbia was allied with Germany
Austria-Hungary contained many Serbs and Croats who might want to join Serbia
Serbia controlled the Ottoman Empire
check.why: As a multi-national empire, Austria-Hungary feared that a strong Serbia would pull its own Slavic peoples away.

check.q: How did the assassination in Sarajevo become a world war?
choices: Austria's ultimatum led to war with Serbia, and the alliance system pulled in Russia, Germany, France and Britain within days
Serbia invaded Austria-Hungary
Britain declared war on Serbia
The Ottoman Empire attacked Russia first
check.why: Each ally honored its promises and its mobilization plans, so a Balkan quarrel drew in every great power in five weeks.

check.q: Why was the war of 1914 a world war rather than a European one?
choices: Because it began in Asia
Because the United States started it
Because the European powers ruled colonies across the globe and drew soldiers from them
Because it was fought entirely at sea
check.why: Empires meant that a war among European states involved India, Africa, Australia, Canada and more from the start.

review.q: What role did Garibaldi play in Italian unification?
choices: He negotiated the alliance with France
He led volunteers who conquered Sicily and Naples, then handed them to the king of Piedmont
He ruled Rome as pope
He commanded the Austrian army
review.why: Garibaldi's thousand red-shirted volunteers took the south in 1860 and he gave his conquests to Victor Emmanuel.

choices: Through three wars led by Prussia under Bismarck
Through a vote of the Frankfurt parliament
Through a treaty with Austria
Through a peaceful union of all German states
review.why: Prussia defeated Denmark, Austria and France in turn, and the German princes proclaimed the Kaiser at Versailles.

review.q: What was the goal of the Meiji leaders' slogan 'rich country, strong army'?
choices: To restore the shogun
To conquer the United States
To close Japan again to foreigners
To modernize Japan so it could not be colonized
review.why: The Meiji government copied Western industry and military methods to keep Japan independent and strong.

review.q: What happened at the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885?
choices: African kings agreed to trade with Europe
European powers set rules for dividing Africa without any African present
Germany gave up its colonies
Ethiopia was recognized as independent
review.why: Fourteen states, all European or American, set the terms of the scramble; no African was invited.

review.q: Why did Ethiopia keep its independence when most of Africa did not?
choices: Europeans were not interested in Ethiopia
Ethiopia had no army
Menelik unified rival lords, bought modern weapons and defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896
Ethiopia was protected by Britain
review.why: Menelik's preparation and his victory at Adwa forced Italy to recognize Ethiopia's independence by treaty.

review.q: What was the main result of the rebellion of 1857 in India?
choices: India became independent
The British Crown replaced the East India Company as ruler of India
The Mughal Empire was restored
The sepoys took over the army
review.why: Parliament abolished company rule in 1858 and began the Raj, direct rule by the Crown.

review.q: What did the unequal treaties forced on China do?
choices: Opened ports, gave foreigners special legal rights, and took territory such as Hong Kong
Ended the opium trade
Made China an equal trading partner
United China and Japan
review.why: Beginning with Nanjing in 1842, the treaties stripped China of control over trade, law and land.

review.q: Why did the alliance system make the 1914 crisis so dangerous?
choices: Because no country had an army
Because the alliances were secret from all leaders
Because Britain refused to join any alliance
Because each power had promised to fight for its allies, so a local war could not stay local
review.why: The Triple Alliance and Triple Entente turned a Balkan quarrel into a war among all the great powers in five weeks.
